newsitem.title: USA: Cigarette tax eyed to fund Minn. Twins stadium.
newsitem.headline: Cigarette tax eyed to fund Minn. Twins stadium.

text.p: A increase of Minnesota's cigarette tax was proposed Wednesday as a way for the state to pay its share of financing a new stadium for the Minnesota Twins baseball team.
Legislative supporters of the outdoor stadium, as well as Gov. Arne Carlson's chief negotiator on the stadium presented the plan at a news conference in St. Paul.
State Rep. Ann Rest, D-New Hope, said a 10 cent per pack increase in the tax would raise $34 million a year for the state's share of the $300 million to $350 million project.

Last week, the Twins owner proposed giving Minnesota a 49 percent stake in the team in return for the state's assistance in financing a new stadium. The team would contribute more than $157.5 million in construction and operating costs for the ballpark.
Rest said the cigarette tax revenues as well as ticket tax revenues at the new ballpark could be tapped to back revenue bonds for the project.

Henry Savelkoul, chairman of the Metropolitan Sports Facilities Commission, who served as Carlson's negotiator, said the cigarette tax hike, which would also raise money for anti-smoking programs, "solves the stadium issue in a responsible manner."
Rest said legislation would be introduced in the next two week.
Still, the plan is likely to run into some opposition.

House Minority Leader Steve Sviggum, R-Kenyon, on Monday unveiled a bill to sell the Metrodome to current tenants the Minnesota Vikings football team and Minnesota Twins baseball team for $1 and allow the teams to keep all revenue generated by the facility.

A spokesman for Sviggum said the lawmaker was opposed to plans to use public financing for a new stadium for the Twins and was offering the bill as an alternative. The bill would also dissolve the Metropolitan Sports Facilities Commission, a state-created agency that operates the Metrodome.
